en: Every morning Sophie went with her mother to the poultry yard, where there were very beautiful hens of different breeds.
Madame de Réan had set some eggs to hatch, which were to produce superb crested hens.
Every day she went with Sophie to see whether the chicks had come out of their eggs.
Sophie carried some bread in a little basket and crumbled it for the hens.
As soon as she arrived, all the hens and all the roosters came running, jumped around her and pecked at the bread almost in her hands and in her basket.
Sophie laughed and ran; the hens followed her, which amused her a lot.
Meanwhile her mother went into a big, beautiful gallery where the hens lived; they were housed like princesses and cared for better than many princesses.
Sophie came to join her when all her bread was crumbled; she watched the little chicks coming out of their shells, which were still too young to run about in the fields.
One morning, when Sophie went into the henhouse, she saw her mother holding a magnificent chick that had been born an hour before.
Oh, what a pretty chick, Mama! Its feathers are as black as a crow's.
Look what a pretty crest it has on its head, too; it will be a magnificent chicken.
Madame de Réan put it back next to the brooding hen.
She had hardly put it down when the hen gave the poor chick a hard peck.
Madame de Réan tapped the nasty hen on the beak, picked up the little chick, which had fallen over crying, and put it back next to the hen.
This time the hen, furious, gave the poor little thing two or three pecks and chased it when it tried to come back.
Madame de Réan rushed over and grabbed the chick, which its mother was about to peck to death.
She made it swallow a drop of water to revive it.
"What are we going to do with this chick?" she said. "It's impossible to leave it with its nasty mother; she would kill it. And yet it's so beautiful that I'd like to raise it.
Listen, Mama, put it in a big basket in the room where my toys are; we'll feed it, and when it's big we'll put it back in the henhouse.
I think you're right; carry it in your bread basket, and let's make it a bed.
Oh, Mama! Look at its neck; it's bleeding, and its back too.
Those are from the hen's pecks; when you've taken it home, ask your nanny for some ointment and put it on its wounds."
Sophie was certainly not pleased to see the chick's wounds, but she was delighted to have to put ointment on them;
so she ran ahead of her mother, showed the chick to her nanny, asked for ointment and put great dollops of it on every spot that was bleeding.
Then she made it a mash of egg, bread and milk, which she crushed and stirred for an hour.
The chick was in pain and sad; it wouldn't eat; it only drank some fresh water several times.
After three days the chick's wounds had healed, and it was walking about in front of the garden steps.
A month later it had become remarkably beautiful and very big for its age;
you would have said it was at least three months old; its feathers were a very rare bluish black, smooth and shiny as if it had just come out of the water.
Its head was covered with an enormous crest of black, orange, blue, red and white feathers.
Its beak and feet were pink; it walked proudly, and its eyes were bright and lively; no one had ever seen a more beautiful chick.
It was Sophie who had taken charge of looking after it; it was she who brought it food; it was she who watched over it when it walked about in front of the house.
In a few days it was to go back to the henhouse, because it was getting too hard to look after.
Sophie sometimes had to run after it for half an hour without being able to catch it;
once it had even nearly drowned by jumping into a pond full of water that it hadn't seen, it was running so fast to get away from Sophie.
She had tried to tie a ribbon round its leg, but it had struggled so much that she had to untie it, for fear it would break its leg.
So her mother forbade her to let it out of the henhouse.
"There are lots of vultures around here that could carry it off; so we must wait until it's big before letting it run free," said Madame de Réan.
But Sophie, who was not obedient, kept letting it out behind her mother's back, and one day, knowing that her mother was busy writing, she brought the chick out in front of the house;
it was having fun looking for gnats and worms in the sand and the grass.
Sophie was combing her doll's hair a few steps away from the chick, looking at it often to stop it wandering off.
Looking up, she was surprised to see a big bird with a hooked beak that had landed three steps from the chick.
It was looking at the chick fiercely, and at Sophie fearfully.
The chick didn't move; it had crouched down and was trembling.
"What a funny bird!" said Sophie.
"It's beautiful, but what a strange look it has! When it looks at me, it seems afraid, and when it looks at the chick, it gives it furious looks!
Ha, ha, ha, how funny it is!"
At that very moment the bird gives a shrill, wild cry, swoops on the chick, which answers with a pitiful cry, seizes it in its claws and carries it off, flying away as fast as it can.
Sophie stood there stunned; her mother, who had come running at the bird's cries, asks Sophie what has happened.
Sophie explains that a bird has carried off the chick, and doesn't understand what it means.
"It means that you are a disobedient little girl, that the bird is a vulture;

that you let it carry off my beautiful chick, which has been killed and eaten by that wicked bird, and that you are going to your room, where you will have your dinner and stay until this evening, to teach you to be more obedient another time."
Sophie hung her head and went sadly to her room; she ate the soup and the meat dish brought to her by her nanny, who loved her and cried to see her cry.
Sophie cried for her poor chick, and missed it for a very long time.
pt: A Sophie ia todas as manhãs com a mãe à capoeira, onde havia galinhas de várias raças, muito bonitas.
A senhora de Réan tinha posto a chocar uns ovos de onde deviam sair galinhas de poupa magníficas.
Todos os dias ia com a Sophie ver se os pintos já tinham saído do ovo.
A Sophie levava num cestinho pão, que esmigalhava para as galinhas.
Assim que chegava, todas as galinhas e todos os galos acorriam, saltavam à volta dela e debicavam o pão quase nas suas mãos e no cesto.
A Sophie ria-se e corria; as galinhas seguiam-na, o que a divertia muito.
Entretanto, a mãe entrava numa galeria grande e bonita onde moravam as galinhas; estavam alojadas como princesas e tratadas melhor do que muitas princesas.
A Sophie ia ter com ela quando tinha esmigalhado o pão todo; via os pintainhos sair da casca, ainda novos demais para correrem pelos campos.
Uma manhã, quando a Sophie entrou no galinheiro, viu a mãe com um pinto magnífico na mão, nascido havia uma hora.
Ah, que pinto tão bonito, mamã! Tem as penas pretas como as de um corvo.
Olha também que poupa tão bonita tem na cabeça; vai ser um frango magnífico.
A senhora de Réan voltou a pô-lo junto da galinha choca.
Mal o tinha pousado, a galinha deu uma grande bicada no pobre pinto.
A senhora de Réan deu uma palmada no bico da galinha má, levantou o pintainho, que tinha caído a piar, e voltou a pô-lo junto da galinha.
Desta vez a galinha, furiosa, deu ao pobrezinho duas ou três bicadas e perseguiu-o quando ele tentou voltar.
A senhora de Réan acorreu e agarrou o pinto, que a mãe ia matar à força de bicadas.
Fê-lo engolir uma gota de água para o reanimar.
— Que vamos fazer a este pinto? — disse ela. — É impossível deixá-lo com a mãe má, ela matava-o; e ele é tão bonito que eu gostava de o criar.
Olhe, mamã, ponha-o num cesto grande, no quarto onde estão os meus brinquedos; damos-lhe de comer e, quando for grande, voltamos a pô-lo no galinheiro.
Acho que tens razão; leva-o no teu cesto do pão, e vamos fazer-lhe uma cama.
Oh, mamã! Olhe para o pescoço dele; está a sangrar, e as costas também.
São as bicadas da galinha; quando o levares para casa, pede à tua ama pomada e põe-lha nas feridas.
A Sophie não estava nada contente por ver o pinto ferido, mas estava encantada por ter de lhe pôr pomada;
correu então à frente da mãe, mostrou o pinto à ama, pediu pomada e pôs-lhe montes dela em cada sítio que sangrava.
Depois preparou-lhe uma papa de ovo, pão e leite, que esmagou e misturou durante uma hora.
O pinto sofria, estava triste, não quis comer; só bebeu várias vezes água fresca.
Ao fim de três dias, as feridas do pinto estavam curadas, e ele passeava em frente da escadaria do jardim.
Um mês depois tinha ficado de uma beleza notável e muito grande para a idade;
dir-se-ia que tinha pelo menos três meses; as penas eram de um preto azulado muito raro, lisas e brilhantes como se tivesse acabado de sair da água.
Tinha a cabeça coberta por uma poupa enorme de penas pretas, cor de laranja, azuis, vermelhas e brancas.
O bico e as patas eram cor-de-rosa; andava com orgulho, os olhos eram vivos e brilhantes; nunca se tinha visto pinto mais bonito.
Tinha sido a Sophie a encarregar-se de tratar dele; era ela que lhe levava de comer; era ela que o guardava quando ele passeava em frente da casa.
Dentro de poucos dias devia voltar para o galinheiro, porque estava a ficar difícil de guardar.
A Sophie às vezes tinha de correr atrás dele meia hora sem o conseguir apanhar;
uma vez até esteve quase a afogar-se, ao atirar-se para um tanque cheio de água que não tinha visto, de tão depressa que corria para fugir da Sophie.
Ela tinha tentado prender-lhe uma fita à pata, mas ele debateu-se tanto que foi preciso soltá-lo, com medo de que partisse a perna.
A mãe proibiu-a então de o deixar sair do galinheiro.
— Há aqui muitos abutres que o podem levar; por isso temos de esperar que seja grande para o deixar em liberdade — disse a senhora de Réan.
Mas a Sophie, que não era obediente, continuava a deixá-lo sair às escondidas da mãe e, um dia, sabendo a mãe ocupada a escrever, levou o pinto para a frente da casa;
ele entretinha-se a procurar mosquitinhos e minhocas na areia e na erva.
A Sophie penteava a boneca a alguns passos do pinto, para quem olhava muitas vezes, para o impedir de se afastar.
Ao levantar os olhos, viu com surpresa uma ave grande de bico curvo que tinha pousado a três passos do pinto.
Olhava para o pinto com ar feroz, e para a Sophie com ar receoso.
O pinto não se mexia; tinha-se encolhido e tremia.
— Que ave tão engraçada! — disse a Sophie.
— É bonita, mas que ar tão esquisito! Quando olha para mim, parece ter medo, e quando olha para o pinto, faz-lhe uns olhos furiosos!
Ah, ah, ah, que engraçada que ela é!
No mesmo instante, a ave solta um grito agudo e selvagem, lança-se sobre o pinto, que responde com um pio lastimoso, agarra-o nas garras e leva-o, voando a toda a velocidade.
A Sophie ficou estupefacta; a mãe, que tinha acorrido aos gritos da ave, pergunta à Sophie o que aconteceu.
A Sophie conta que uma ave levou o pinto, e não percebe o que isso quer dizer.
— Quer dizer que és uma desobediente, que a ave é um abutre;

que o deixaste levar o meu belo pinto, que foi morto e devorado por aquela ave má, e que vais já para o teu quarto, onde vais jantar e ficar até à noite, para aprenderes a ser mais obediente de outra vez.
A Sophie baixou a cabeça e foi tristemente para o quarto; jantou a sopa e o prato de carne que lhe levou a ama, que gostava dela e chorava de a ver chorar.
A Sophie chorava o seu pobre pinto, de quem teve saudades durante muito tempo.
